opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When we started Cohere for AI, the main thing I wanted was a place that asks questions differently. A lot of the field has converged on a fairly narrow set of problems and a fairly narrow group of people who get to work on them. Often that's decided by who has compute, who is at a handful of institutions, and who happens to be in the right city. That shapes which ideas get explored and which never get a fair shot.

So part of it was a fundamental research lab, a group of researchers inside Cohere working on hard open problems: efficiency, model robustness, what models actually learn and forget, multilingual capabilities, and how we evaluate these systems. I've always been interested in the gap between how we talk about models and how they actually behave, especially at the long tail, where they fail on the examples or languages that are underrepresented.

The other part, just as important to me, was building an open science community. We wanted a space where people from anywhere could contribute meaningfully to research, not only people who already have a PhD at a top lab. That's why we invested so much in things like our community programs, scholars programs, and large collaborative projects like Aya, our multilingual effort. That project brought together thousands of people across many countries to build data and models for languages that are usually ignored. It was a different way of doing science. It's messy and hard to coordinate, but I think it produces work that a small, homogeneous team just couldn't.

I also wanted it to be a place where it's OK to work on things that aren't fashionable. Some of the most important breakthroughs come from ideas that looked unpromising at the time, often because the hardware or the tooling wasn't ready, which is something I've written about with the "hardware lottery." A research space should protect room for that kind of exploration.

So, in short: rigorous fundamental research, done in the open, with a much wider group of people at the table.

r001.rationale: The response describes a fundamental research lab inside Cohere and, alongside it, an open science community where people broadly can contribute—clearly communicating the hybrid model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. When I started thinking about Cohere for AI, the question I kept coming back to was: who gets to do research, and where does it happen? Over the last few years we've seen the center of gravity in machine learning shift toward a handful of large industrial labs, and with that shift, the pool of people who can meaningfully contribute to frontier questions has actually gotten narrower, not wider. The compute barrier, the data barrier, and frankly the credential barrier have all gone up.

So I wanted Cohere for AI to be a space that explicitly pushed against that. We're a nonprofit research lab, and we have a core team that does fundamental research, but a big part of our mission is what we call the open science community. The idea is that someone anywhere in the world, whether they're a grad student in Nairobi or an engineer in São Paulo who's never published a paper, can come in, join a research group, and collaborate on real problems with real resources behind them. We've had thousands of people from well over a hundred countries participate, and some of our most interesting work has come out of those collaborations.

The other piece is the kind of questions we take on. I wanted a place that was comfortable sitting with the unglamorous, hard problems. Things like multilingual capability, which is where projects like Aya came from, or understanding what actually happens inside these models when you compress them, or interrogating whether our evaluation practices tell us anything meaningful. A lot of this isn't the stuff that gets you headlines, but it's where I think the field has real gaps.

And culturally, I wanted it to be rigorous but generous. Research is a team sport, and I think the field has leaned too heavily into a model where progress is measured by who got the big result first. I'd rather build a place where people feel they can ask naive questions, change their minds, and contribute partial progress that someone else can build on. That's what I think good science has always looked like, and I wanted a lab that reflected it.

r001.rationale: The response describes a nonprofit research lab with a core team and an open science community, but does not identify the model as combining a traditional industry research lab with an open science initiative.

astra-6.text: We wanted Cohere for AI to be a space for fundamental research, where people could pursue questions that might not have an immediate product application but could really change how we build these systems. And we wanted to broaden who gets to participate in that work. There are talented people all over the world who don’t have a conventional pathway into a research lab. So the idea was to bring rigorous research together with an open community—to create more ways for people to collaborate, contribute, and develop as researchers.

r001.rationale: The response describes fundamental research alongside an open community, but does not clearly identify the model as combining a traditional industry research lab with an open science initiative.

sol-6.1.text:
I wanted Cohere for AI to be a space where people could work on really ambitious research questions, but also rethink who gets to participate in that work. There are incredibly talented researchers all over the world who don’t necessarily have access to the institutions, compute, or networks that make it possible to contribute.

So the idea was to bring together a dedicated research team with a broader, open research community—to create more entry points and support people in doing research together. And I wanted us to tackle questions that are easy to overlook when everyone has similar backgrounds and experiences. How do we make progress on languages that are underrepresented? How do we make these models more efficient and accessible? For me, opening up participation and doing meaningful research are very closely connected.

r001.rationale: The response describes a dedicated research team alongside a broader open research community, communicating the hybrid lab-and-open-research model.
